relations.note: Carmenta is consistently identified as Evander’s mother in the developed legend.

relations.myth: Evander’s exile and migration to Latium
relations.note: She counsels Evander, shares his exile, guides him to Latium, and predicts his future.
Hermes fathers Evander by Carmenta in a Greek genealogy later amplified by medieval mythographers.
Dionysius and Plutarch report Themis as Carmenta’s Greek or former name.

relations.myth: Paired Carmentes governing birth and temporal knowledge
relations.note: Prorsa is Carmenta’s counterpart or divided aspect, governing head-first birth or knowledge of the past.

relations.myth: Paired Carmentes governing birth and temporal knowledge
relations.note: Postverta is Carmenta’s counterpart or divided aspect, governing reverse birth or knowledge of the future.
Carmenta changes fifteen Greek letters into Latin forms, while Apollo supplies the remaining letters.
Carmenta directs the Arcadian settlers to establish a sanctuary dedicated to Pan Lycaeus.
Carmenta’s Arcadian settlers establish Victory’s precinct during the settlement of Pallantium.
Ovid commemorates both goddesses on 11 January, without describing an interaction or shared rite.

relations.myth: Comparison of forward and backward divine sight
relations.note: Macrobius compares Janus’ double sight with the temporal knowledge of Carmenta’s paired aspects.

relations.myth: Prophecy of Hercules’ arrival in Latium
relations.note: Carmenta prophetically anticipates events connected with Hercules’ future arrival in Latium.
Carmenta foretells the greatness of Aeneas’ descendants; Evander later shows Aeneas her altar.
Plutarch reports an interpretation identifying Carmenta as one of the Fates.
